title: What ML/LLM models are you using and for what?
author: AoideusWasBanned
selftext:
\- Guessing price?

\- Guessing direction?

\- Guessing volatility?

\- Guessing regime?

\- Categorizing assets??

If not too private, I'd love to learn what models you guys are already using and for what purposes you're using them. Oh nd all these applies to LLM modes as well.

All replies are much appreciated. Thanks in advance.

comments.author: Square-Middle-4474
comments.body:
First Item. I do not guess, I estimate risk using basic parametric statistics

Second I can use any LLM but am using google currently. In my opinion the specific model does not matter. It is more important for the user to know how to prompt. Without that skill all the models fail

Finally, I use AI to gather and normalize data, and to present a basic summary format which I check myself. Once I have edited the result, I recast it in my own language with corrections. Currently I am using AI to gather data on pending High Impact Economic Reports. I also use it to gather raw data from the Options Exchange so that I can obtain updated information as to the location of Put/Call "Walls" as well as the location of the Gamma Flip.

Yesterday's New York Session was an excellent example.  I created an updated OI model about an hour after the open, and it pointed to a put wall at 7600. As the day wore on that model changed and I was able to adjust it down about 20 points. That adjusted level is where price ended up, providing an accurate profit target for my short position.

replies.author: pigeon_shit
replies.body:
The distinction:

**Guess:** "I think this stock is going to go up."

**Hypothesis:** "This stock tends to rise following a 5% pullback when trading volume remains below its 20-day average."

**Tested hypothesis:** You collect historical data, define the conditions, and test whether the pattern actually produces a measurable advantage.  
A hypothesis doesn't have to be correct. In fact, it can be completely wrong.

**The key distinction is that a hypothesis is structured to be tested and potentially disproven.**

comments.author: QuanTradin
comments.body:
mostly not price. what's held up is narrower than the list.

volatility is where plain models earn their keep, since vol clusters and even GARCH or a boosted tree on realized vol does better than guessing. direction from price alone has looked like a coin flip in most honest out-of-sample tests I've seen.

regime I treat as a filter, not a prediction: a simple trend and volatility state that decides whether a rule is allowed to trade at all that day.

LLMs get the boring jobs: turning a written rule into code, turning filings or headlines into labels, and reading a strategy description for terms nobody defined. I wouldn't let one guess a price.

whatever the model, the test that matters is walk-forward on data it never saw, with costs in. most of the impressive ones die right there.

comments.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
comments.body: I don't run these myself, so I can only say what tends to hold up. Volatility and regime work usually do better than price or direction, since volatility clusters and is easier to forecast than where price goes next. For any of them, I'd compare against a simple baseline like rolling volatility or a basic moving average, on data the model never saw, and after fees. LLMs are more useful for sorting news and organizing research than for predicting price. Cymetica's Backtest Labs has a fee setting and a held out stretch of data for that kind of check.

comments.author: slypleasure33139
comments.body:
I am rather new to the current environment of AI, and your question is a similar question I had back in the late 80's, so I might have a general answer that points you in the right direction. 

1. I am for all intents and purposes a system/systematic trader. 
2. I designed and still use expert systems concepts based on historical data to find my investment opportunities. 
3. My systems are now on spreadsheets instead of notepads and index cards.
4. my oldest system is 40ish years active, and my most current is the pre-cursor or a simultaneously discovered that is very similar to the MACD-V which was publicly spoken about first. 

I think that most models that have deeper technical knowledge of the markets should be able to help you create an "agent" that performs most of the filtering needed to give you a solid output. 

I happen to use CANSLIM now for almost 40 years, it's got a few filters, and one of my " agents " jobs is to filter out all the stocks under 5.00 and trade more than 1 million shares a day, so out of a basic universe of 3200 different stocks, about 600-720 show up daily ( no etfs, no preferred ). then I have other " agents " work the rest of the filtering. 

In my journeys with AI, I have slowly tried and with great failure, implemented agents, to watch it fail spectacularly. And I have learned a great deal IE: I'm not really gifted at it yet. Like flying a plane, the hard stuff is easy, the easy stuff is hard. 

Do I have volatility " agents " and market/individual stock directions " agents ", Yes. I also have all my stocks within there business sector and have charts of the business cycles and economic cycles of the USA, Canada, EU overall and separate countries. I usually trade long and with the business cycle of the correct sector. 

my spreadsheets works and claude is struggling, but I am very sure that it's my lack of skills making it hard.

comments.author: drguid
comments.body:
LightGBM and GAM.

What works? A good buy signal + a ML model to boost the win rate a bit. i.e. find something with a 51% win rate then filter out trades so it has a 60% win rate. That will go from OK profitability to godlike profitability.

comments.author: logicalJunkie549
comments.body:
So ML is nothing new to the quantitative finance industry at all - any supervised trees ML (LightGBM or XGboost are the frequent ones used in this space). Just remember to be almost paranoid of overfitting (thats kinda what machine learning does if you think about it lol). 
Problem with LLM's - you cant backtest this reliably at all, (LLM's know what happened in the past if you backtest it). 

Good luck mate
